extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, ethics counsel, and disciplinary adjudicators at the USPTO (OED/PTAB)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for evaluating whether a patent practitioner violated USPTO disciplinary rules (esp. 37 C.F.R. §10.23) by creating, introducing, or using fabricated or misleading documents (e.g., in interference/deposition proceedings). Covers when items are 'in evidence', intent, demonstrative aids, notice/amendment rules, and related burdens of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a document is 'in evidence' before the Board
rubrics_metrics.description: A document is 'in evidence' before the Board only if it was filed with the Board in support of a motion, opposition or reply or as an exhibit for the final hearing; mere submission to a court reporter or listing on an exhibit list without filing does not make it 'in evidence'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhibits must be filed with the Board under the Standing Order at the specified time; an exhibit listed but noted 'exhibit not submitted' is not treated as evidence. Example: GX 2195 was not 'in evidence' for substantive priority issues until submitted by Chiron in support of its motion for sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent requirement for 'knowingly use ... evidence' (37 C.F.R. §10.858(a)(4),(a)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner cannot 'knowingly use . . . evidence' or 'participate in the creation ... of evidence when the practitioner knows or it is obvious that the evidence is false' if at the time of creation/use the item was not contemplated or intended by that person to be used as evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge requires intent to use the item as evidence at the time of creation/use; creating a document for another purpose (e.g., demonstrative aid) supports lack of intent to create false evidence. The timing of intent is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'fabricated evidence'
rubrics_metrics.description: "[F]alse or deceitful evidence that is unlawfully created, usu[ally] after the relevant event, in an attempt to avoid liability or conviction." (Black's Law Dictionary)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This dictionary definition supports the view that evidence fabricated for purposes other than being used as evidence may not fit the ordinary meaning of 'fabricated evidence' unless intended as such.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing Order / authentication requirements for exhibits and scientific data
rubrics_metrics.description: Standing Order §43 requires a party who is relying on scientific data to explain, through testimony of a witness, why the data is being relied upon, how the test is performed, how the data is used to determine a value, and other information; exhibits should be authenticated if they are to be considered evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to comply with these requirements (e.g., failing to authenticate or offer testimony explaining data) weighs against treating an exhibit as submitted evidence. Respondent's failure to comply with such requirements undermined any claim GX 2195 was a relied-on scientific exhibit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between demonstrative aids and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrative aids (duplicates, models, sketches, mock-ups, modified excerpts) are typically not themselves evidence and may be used to make interrogation more effective, subject to limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court decisions allow demonstratives to test bias or clarify testimony (e.g., Fed. R. Civ. P. 611(a); United States v. Taylor; United States v. Burt), but they exceed proper purpose where the factfinder would confuse them with reality (e.g., Harris v. Poppel). Use as demonstrative aids is permissible if not offered to convince the factfinder of their truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (Rule 10.23(b)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 10.23(b)(4) provides that a practitioner shall not 'engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.' Subsection 10.23(d) provides that reckless indifference to the truth is chargeable as knowledge; deceitful half-truths or concealment of material facts may be deemed actual fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violation elements require showing practitioner engaged in conduct involving those acts. Reckless indifference can substitute for actual knowledge; concealment with intent to mislead may constitute misrepresentation under these rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common‑law/dictionary definitions applied to 'dishonesty' and 'misrepresentation'
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the Rules do not define 'dishonesty' or 'misrepresentation', their common dictionary meanings govern: 'dishonest' = lack of truth/trustworthiness; 'misrepresentation' = a false or misleading assertion (including conduct or concealment) usually with intent to deceive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concealment or non-disclosure that amounts to a false assertion can violate Rule 10.23(b)(4); courts and ethics opinions (e.g., Floyd) apply these definitions when evaluating practitioner conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: No rule-based exception permitting fabrication to test witness bias
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no exception in the Rules, analogous state ethics rules, or directly on-point case law or bar opinions permitting a practitioner to create or introduce fabricated documents during deposition or cross‑examination solely to test an expert's bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance cases (Metzger, Thoreen, Friedman, Statzer) counsel against such tactics. While practitioners may argue unsettled law or policy arguments (e.g., Terry), absence of an explicit exception means the conduct remains subject to discipline analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to be truthful to opposing counsel and not continue misrepresentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorneys have an ongoing duty to be truthful to opposing counsel; continuing a misrepresentation (e.g., equivocal answers in email correspondence, misleading statements to opposing counsel or the Board) can constitute dishonesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (Goodman, Griffith, Miskovsky) supports that post-deposition communications that perpetuate false impressions may be unethical; the timing and content of communications are relevant to assessing continued deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'False evidence' is not a necessary element of Rules 10.23(b)(4),(b)(5),(b)(6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the Complaint refers to 'false evidence' (as a reference to a particular exhibit), the existence of 'false evidence' is not an element required to prove violations of Rules 10.23(b)(4), (b)(5), or (b)(6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The words 'false evidence' in a complaint may refer to specific described facts rather than a legal element. Administrative disciplinary proceedings are not criminal; agency rules (37 C.F.R. §10.145) permit amendment to conform to evidence and courts assess whether the respondent had notice and opportunity to respond (Ruffalo; Zauderer; related cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency pleading and amendment-to-conform standard (37 C.F.R. §10.145)
rubrics_metrics.description: In case of variance between evidence and allegations, the administrative law judge may amend the complaint to conform to the evidence; any party prejudiced by amendment must be given reasonable opportunity to meet the amended allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleadings in administrative proceedings are judged by notice standards rather than strict criminal indictment rules; amendment is appropriate where respondent had notice of the nature of the charges and an opportunity to litigate them. Relevant authorities: Citizens State Bank v. FDIC, Zauderer, In re Ruffalo, and related disciplinary decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors and evidence relevant to determining intent to create/use an item as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Intent may be inferred from creation and presentation context: markings and edits made to give 'flavor of authenticity', showing a document to a witness and asking leading questions implying it is definitive, failure to authenticate or describe it as demonstrative, and subsequent communications with opposing counsel or the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony that the item was created as a demonstrative aid, contemporaneous filings/motions, objections by opposing counsel, and whether the item was filed with the Board are all relevant. The record must show intent by clear and convincing evidence to find creation/use as false evidence for disciplinary purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibitions in Rule 10.23(b)(5) and (b)(6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 10.23(b)(5) prohibits engaging in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice; Rule 10.23(b)(6) prohibits engaging in conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions are distinct prohibitions that, like (b)(4), do not require 'false evidence' as a formal element; findings under these rules consider whether conduct undermines justice or fitness to practice, and may be based on the same underlying facts as (b)(4).
